Ground 1 - Contractual obligations regarding waterproofing

The appellant’s case was that, by reason of the specific contractual terms: “waterproofing membrane to sill to be provided by builder”; and that the appellant was “responsible for waterproofing of our windows only. If structure is not waterproofed correctly, warranties are voided”, the appellant was not responsible for the installation of flashing around the windows.

The respondents submitted that the terms of the contract were superseded by the Deed. The respondents relied upon clause 14 of the Deed which provided:

14. Entire agreement

This Deed

14.1 constitutes the entire agreement between the parties as to its subject matter; and

14.2 in relation to that subject matter, supersedes any prior understanding or agreement between the parties and any prior condition, warranty, indemnity or representation imposed, given or made by a party.

In reply, the appellant referred to clause 7 of the Deed which we have set out at [6] above. The appellant submitted that clause 7 preserved the terms of the original contract, and that clause 14, properly construed, was intended “to avoid arguments that pre-Deed negotiations, oral representations and correspondence could form part of the Deed or affect its construction”.

The Tribunal addressed the appellant’s submissions regarding the contractual obligations relating to waterproofing at [57] as follows:

The respondents raise, by way of defence, that the windows failed because the builder, Mr Bannister, failed to install the window flashings in accordance with good building practice and that the builder’s failure to install flashing is causative of the leaks in all three windows and therefore causative of the applicant’s loss. I accept and prefer the expert evidence of Mr Brennan in his report of 17 May 2020 that it was the responsibility of the window supplier to “flash the building element to avoid moisture egress between the window frame and the house frame” and accept that the report of Mr Sim in respect of the flashing should be disregarded because the Schlegel Test Mr Sim considered is “irrelevant to the windows fitted on site into a timber frame with light weight external cladding”. On balance where Mr Brennan and Mr Sim differ on the issue of flashing, I accept and prefer the opinion of Mr Brennan as the more experienced expert in respect of window manufacture and installation. I also find that as Mr Sim adopted the wrong Schlegel Test, his opinion is not as persuasive.

Reference to the respective experts’ reports is necessary to understand that conclusion.

Mr Brennan’s opinion was that the windows leaked both by reason of the absence of small joint sealer and by reason of the absence of flashing around the windows.

Mr Sim’s opinion was that there was small joint sealer and that flashing of the windows was unnecessary. In support of the proposition that flashing was unnecessary Mr Sim stated that “the windows [are] manufactured from commercial grade sections and used sub-heads and sub-sills which act [as] a flashing”.

Mr Sim also stated “there is no requirement for additional flashing to the head, jambs or sills of this type of window, if installed in the correct manner as per the Schlegel Test Report.”

The Schlegel Test Report was a test report issued by Schlegel Pty Ltd, an NATA accredited laboratory, which certified the performance of a sample window. The test was carried out in 2010.

Mr Brennan’s evidence in reply was that testing in a “Schlegel portable test rig” did not extend to flashing as:

…there are many varied building structures by which windows and doors need to be assembled into, so it is impossible to test in all building envelope constructions…

The Tribunal’s conclusion that Mr Brennan’s evidence should be preferred to the evidence of Mr Sim was a finding of fact. Clearly the Tribunal determined that the windows required flashing and that flashing had not been installed.

The conclusion that it was the responsibility of the window supplier to “flash the building element to avoid moisture egress between the window frame and the house frame” was based upon the statement in paragraph 4.5 of Mr Brennan’s reply report that:

…Sub heads, sub jambs, and sub/sump sills are a means of installation usually used in commercial shop front and residential concrete construction. They do not substitute for flashing at any time, but especially when a cavity wall construction or timber frame light weight cladding is used. If you are using all these elements to install, you still need to flash to the building element to avoid moisture egress between the window frame and the house frame, through to internal wall surfaces.

Mr Brennan did not state that it was the responsibility of the window supplier and installer to “flash to the building element”, only that it was necessary to install flashing. However, Mr Brennan did state in his oral evidence that the flashing of a window was part of the installation of the window rather than preparation of the opening for the installation of the window.

In rejecting the appellant’s submission that any leakage arising from the absence of flashing was the responsibility of the builder and not the appellant, the Tribunal does not appear to have considered the question whether the contractual provisions relating to responsibility for waterproofing cast the responsibility to install flashing on the builder, or if so, whether those provisions were superseded by the Deed.

However, the Tribunal determined that the windows leaked by reason of the absence of small joint sealant and concluded on that basis that the windows were defective and required replacement.

Accordingly, the question who was responsible for the installation of flashing was not relevant to the question whether the appellant was responsible for the cost of replacement of the windows. The fact that the absence of flashing might have contributed to the extent of leakage could not alter the conclusion that the windows were defective.

Accordingly, ground 1 must be rejected. It involves neither an error of law nor a conclusion that was not fair and equitable or against the weight of evidence.

We reach this conclusion independently of the question whether clause 14 of the Deed, properly construed, excluded reference to the terms of the original contract. However, it is clear in our view that, in light of the explicit provision in clause 7 of the Deed, clause 14 cannot be construed as excluding reference to the terms of the original contract in ascertaining the extent of the appellant’s obligations.

To create a block in AutoCAD using Python, you can use the `acad.model.AddBlock` method. This method takes the following arguments:

* `block_name`: The name of the block to be created.

* `objects`: A list of objects that make up the block. These objects can be any 2D or 3D geometric object, such as lines, circles, arcs, or surfaces.

import autocad

# Define the block name and insertion point
block_name = "myblock"
base_point = (0, 0, 0)

# Define the objects that make up the block

line3 = acad.model.AddLine((1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 0))
line4 = acad.model.AddLine((0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 0))
objects = [line1, line2, line3, line4]

# Create the block
acad.model.AddBlock(block_name, base_point, objects)
```

List the layers of the TCP/IP model and for each layer identify one protocol.

The TCP/IP model consists of four layers, each responsible for a specific aspect of network communication. The layers and their corresponding protocols are:

1. Application Layer: This layer is responsible for providing applications with access to network services. Examples of protocols at this layer include HTTP, FTP, SMTP, and DNS.
2. Transport Layer: This layer is responsible for providing reliable data transfer between applications. Examples of protocols at this layer include TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol).
3. Internet Layer: This layer is responsible for addressing and routing data between networks. The main protocol at this layer is the Internet Protocol (IP).
4. Link Layer: This layer is responsible for transmitting data over a physical network link. Examples of protocols at this layer include Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol).

It's worth noting that while the TCP/IP model is often used as a reference for networking, it is not the only model in use. The OSI model is another commonly referenced networking model that consists of seven layers.

An application server, on the other hand, is a program that provides a platform for developing and deploying software applications. Distinguish between a library and a framework giving examples

A library and a framework are both reusable pieces of code that can help developers to build software applications more efficiently. However, there are some key differences between the two.

A library is a collection of pre-written code that provides specific functionality that can be used by an application. It typically consists of a set of functions, classes, or modules that a developer can call from within their own code to perform specific tasks. Examples of libraries include NumPy, React, and jQuery.

In contrast, a framework is a more comprehensive tool that provides a structured approach to building applications. It includes a set of pre-defined rules, conventions, and components that help developers to build applications more quickly and with fewer errors. Unlike a library, which provides specific functionality, a framework provides a general structure for the entire application. Examples of frameworks include Ruby on Rails, Django, and AngularJS.

The key difference between a library and a framework is the level of control that the developer has over the application. With a library, the developer is in control of the overall structure of the application and can choose which functions to use from the library. With a framework, the developer must adhere to the structure and conventions of the framework, and the framework handles much of the underlying logic of the application.

To further illustrate the difference, consider a scenario where a developer wants to build a web application that involves data visualization. They could use a library like D3.js to create interactive charts and graphs, and incorporate them into their own custom web application. In contrast, if they wanted to build the entire web application using a framework, they might choose something like Ruby on Rails or Django, which provide a complete structure for building web applications, including models, views, and controllers.

In summary, while both libraries and frameworks are useful tools for developers, the key difference lies in the level of control they offer and the scope of the tasks they can help to accomplish. A library provides specific functionality, while a framework provides a structure for building an entire application.

Explain what happens when an HTTP request is made

When an HTTP request is made, the following steps take place:

1. DNS lookup: The domain name in the URL is resolved to an IP address using the Domain Name System (DNS). This allows the client to locate the server that hosts the website.
2. TCP connection: The client establishes a TCP connection with the server. This involves a three-way handshake where the client sends a SYN message to the server, the server responds with a SYN-ACK message, and the client sends an ACK message back to the server. This establishes a reliable, bi-directional communication channel between the client and the server.
3. HTTP request: The client sends an HTTP request to the server using the TCP connection. The request typically includes a method (such as GET or POST), a URL, headers, and a body (for POST requests). The headers may include information about the client, such as the user agent and any cookies that have been set.
4. Server processing: The server receives the HTTP request and processes it. This typically involves parsing the request, looking up the requested resource (such as a web page or an image) on the server's file system or in a database, and generating a response.
5. HTTP response: The server sends an HTTP response back to the client using the same TCP connection. The response typically includes a status code (such as 200 OK or 404 Not Found), headers (including any cookies that the server wants to set), and a body (containing the requested resource or an error message).
6. Client processing: The client receives the HTTP response and processes it. This typically involves parsing the response, checking the status code to determine if the request was successful or not, and rendering the response to the user (such as displaying a web page or an image).
7. TCP connection teardown: Once the HTTP response has been received and processed, the client and server tear down the TCP connection. This involves a four-way handshake where the client sends a FIN message to the server, the server responds with a FIN-ACK message, the server sends a FIN message back to the client, and the client responds with a FIN-ACK message. This releases the resources that were allocated for the connection and allows both the client and server to move on to other tasks.

Overall, the HTTP request process allows clients to communicate with servers over the internet and retrieve resources such as web pages, images, and other types of data.

3. The render props pattern, which allows you to share logic across components using a prop that specifies a function to render the component. This can make your code more flexible and reusable.

Consequences Affect Learning

There are numerous data preprocessing techniques. Data cleaning can be applied to remove
noise and correct inconsistencies in data. Data integration merges data from multiple sources
into a coherent data store such as a data warehouse. Data reduction can reduce data size by,
for instance, aggregating, eliminating redundant features, or clustering.
Data transformations (e.g., normalization) may be applied, where data are
scaled to fall within a smaller range like 0.0 to 1.0.
Data Quality: Why Preprocess the Data?
Data have quality if they satisfy the requirements of the intended use. There are many
factors comprising data quality, including
a. accuracy,
b. completeness,
c. consistency,
d. timeliness,
e. believability, and
f. interpretability. There are many possible reasons for inaccurate data (i.e., having incorrect attribute values).
1. The data collection instruments used may be faulty.
2. There may have been human or computer errors occurring at data entry.
3. Users may purposely submit incorrect data values for mandatory fields when they do
not wish to submit personal information (e.g., by choosing the default value “January
1” displayed for birthday). This is known as disguised missing data. 4. Errors in data transmission can also occur. There may be technology limitations such
as limited buffer size for coordinating synchronized data transfer and consumption.
Incorrect data may also result from inconsistencies in naming conventions or data codes, or inconsistent formats for input fields (e.g., date). Duplicate tuples also require data
cleaning.
Incomplete data can occur for a number of reasons.
Other data may not be included simply because they were not considered important at the time
of entry. Relevant data may not be recorded due to a misunderstanding or because of equipment
malfunctions.
Data that were inconsistent with other recorded data may have been deleted.
The recording of the data history or modifications may have been overlooked. Missing
data, particularly for tuples with missing values for some attributes, may need to be
inferred.
Timeliness also affects data quality. Suppose that you are overseeing the
distribution of monthly sales bonuses to the top sales representatives at AllElectronics. Several sales representatives, however, fail to submit their sales records on time at the
end of the month. There are also a number of corrections and adjustments that flow in
after the month’s end. For a period of time following each month, the data stored in
the database are incomplete. However, once all of the data are received, it is correct.
The fact that the month-end data are not updated in a timely fashion has a negative
impact on the data quality.
Believability reflects how much the data are trusted by users.
Interpretability reflects how easy the data are understood.
Suppose that a database, at one point, had several errors, all of which have since been
corrected. The past errors, however, had caused many problems for sales department
users, and so they no longer trust the data. The data also use many accounting codes,
which the sales department does not know how to interpret. Even though the database is
now accurate, complete, consistent, and timely, sales department users may regard it as

* Data preprocessing techniques include data cleaning, integration, reduction, and transformations like normalization.
* Data quality is important for data to be useful, and it includes factors like accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, believability, and interpretability.
* Inaccurate data can result from faulty instruments, errors during data entry, purposely submitting incorrect data, and errors in data transmission.
* Incomplete data can result from missing information or equipment malfunctions, among other reasons.
* Timeliness affects data quality, and delays in updating data can negatively impact data quality.
* Believability reflects how much the data are trusted by users, and interpretability reflects how easily the data can be understood.

Data Reduction
Consider that we have selected data from the AllElectronics data warehouse for analysis. The
data set will likely be huge. Complex data analysis and mining on huge amounts of data can
take a long time, making such analysis impractical or infeasible.
Data reduction techniques can be applied to obtain a reduced representation of the data set
that is much smaller in volume, yet closely maintains the integrity of the original data. That is,
mining on the reduced data set should be more efficient yet produce the same (or almost the
same) analytical results.
Data reduction strategies include
1. Dimensionality reduction, 2. Numerosity reduction, and
3. Data compression. Dimensionality reduction is the process of reducing the number of random variables or

Social and political changes in the 1980s and planning of the 1992 textbooks
The dominant thrust of China’s post-Mao education reforms was towards pursuit of the “four modernizations” through the reinstitution of radically elitist structures and selective mechanisms. Education, declared Deng Xiaoping, must “face modernization, the world and the future”. At the same time, however, reconfiguring the party’s legitimating narrative for the post-Mao era meant that facing up to the past – especially the recent past – could not be entirely avoided. The CCP Central Committee attempted to resolve lingering intra-party divisions in 1981, with a “Resolution on certain questions in the history of our party,” which publicly acknowledged “mistakes,” and assessed Mao’s legacy as “seven parts good and three parts bad” (Vickers & Zeng, 2017, p. 41).

But while striving to heal its own internal wounds, in the 1980s the CCP also faced the difficult task of restoring its legitimacy amongst non-Han minorities, whose culture, heritage and way of life had been subjected to particularly vicious attack from radical Maoists. In tandem with a more general relaxation of overt political indoctrination, the CCP loosened constraints on cultural (and religious) expression, emphasizing the principle of “equality among ethnic groups” (民族平等). The liberal wing of the new leadership under Hu Yaobang (1915–1989) believed that tolerance of minorities and recognition of their cultures could help rebuild their loyalty, which would eventually be cemented by the benefits of modernization (Bass, 1998; Hawkins, 1983).7 The introduction of policies and laws to strengthen protection for the cultural and religious rights of minorities was seen as an urgent priority (Bass, 1998). The Nationalities and Regional Autonomy Law (民族区域自治法), enacted in 1984, featured strengthened language on the protection of minorities’ “cultural autonomy”. Meanwhile, concerns to maintain control over “border areas” inhabited by minorities dictated preferential funding for schooling there, even while budgets were squeezed elsewhere (Vickers & Zeng, 2017, p. 40). This included support for bilingual provision in the more junior grades and, from 1985, provision of secondary schooling in “inland” regions for students from Tibet (内地西藏班), and later from Xinjiang (Chen, 2008).

Supporting the shift in official “minorities” policy, in 1988 Fei Xiaotong, the eminent ethnographer and vice-chair of the National People’s Congress, proposed a conception of Chinese nationhood characterized by a “pattern of diversity in unity” (多元一体格局). He expounded this in a talk delivered in Hong Kong, where Beijing was separately seeking to reassure nervous locals of its pluralist credentials. It was subsequently invoked as a guiding principle in official policy and in academic papers on ethnic relations. Although Fei stressed the “oneness” (一体) of the Chinese people and the core (核心) status of the Han, he emphasized China’s multi-ethnic origins and called for more research in this area (Fei, 2003).8

The 1988 draft Outline for History at junior secondary level, on the basis of which the 1992 textbooks were compiled, thus emerged out of a political climate marked by relative liberalism, and a conciliatory official line on Han-minority relations.9 For the first time, a small but fixed proportion of class hours (5%) was allotted specifically to the teaching of ethnic minority or local history, “the teaching of which had hitherto been sporadic” (Jones, 2005, p. 87). Overall, the Outline manifested a “demotion of theory” that Jones attributes in part to trends in professional historical research, which during the 1980s was increasingly open to influences from overseas (especially America). With the “straitjacket” of historical materialism loosening, attention to themes such as class struggle and peasant risings declined, with a greater focus instead on culture and the role of “Great Men” (ibid., p. 87). On the issue of ethnicity, the Outline states:

Our country is a unified multi-ethnic country wherein the Han are the majority. The history of our motherland is made by all ethnicities.10 History teaching needs not only to teach the history and contribution of the Han, but also those of minority ethnicities. The equality among ethnic groups, the safeguarding of national unity and inter-ethnic solidarity are the principles for dealing with ethnic issues in history teaching. The people of all ethnic groups developed close political, economic and cultural links throughout history. They not only engaged in friendly exchanges and contributed to the construction of the motherland together, but also together resisted class oppression and foreign aggression. (MOE, 1988, p. 3)

While emphasizing national unity, the 1988 syllabus thus also promoted a multi-ethnic narrative and stressed the principle of inter-ethnic equality.

According to RICT (2010, p. 291), this Outline was drafted mainly by PEP editors, though other scholars, including some from the Central College of Nationalities (中央民族学院) participated in an advisory capacity. One editor involved was Wang Hongzhi, later the leading chief editor of the 1992 history texts (Wang, 2000, p. 420). The representation of non-Han minority groups in school textbooks was a long-standing interest for Wang, which she attributed partly to an encounter earlier in the 1980s with Mongolian educators dissatisfied with textbook glorification of the Han general Yue Fei (岳飞, 1103–1142), traditionally regarded as “national hero” for his exploits resisting the Jurchen (女真族, forerunners of the Manchus) (ibid., p. 659).11 She claimed this had taught her that historical writing should “abandon the traditional bias of big (i.e. Han) nationalism and fully value the status and role of minority ethnicities in the historical development of the motherland,” which belonged equally to all members of China’s “great multi-ethnic family” (ibid.).

In her academic work, Wang projected the multi-ethnic reality of contemporary China backwards to the ancient past. In doing so, she cited as a chief inspiration her undergraduate teacher Jian Bozan (1898–1968) (Wang, 2000, pp. 218–9, 661), the eminent Uyghur Marxist who helped the CCP to develop a multi-ethnic narrative of China’s history (Leibold, 2007).12 In 1961, Jian had written:

… when we write Chinese history, we should be aware of not separating the history of the Han from the history of other ethnicities in China.… Do not treat these non-Han ethnic groups as foreign. Regardless of their relations with the central regime, we should acknowledge those ancient ethnic groups which inhabited modern Chinese territory as Chinese. (Jian, 1961)

Wang had been involved to varying degrees in compiling previous editions of PEP’s history textbooks since the late 1970s (RICT, 2010).13 As Jones notes, in these post-Mao texts “ethnic relations and national unity … featured more prominently” than previously, “presumably to counteract secessionist and anti-Chinese sentiment … exacerbated by Cultural Revolution excesses” (2005, p. 81). The curricular Outlines of the late 1970s included “eradicating ethnic chauvinism and localism” as a curricular objective, but this had disappeared by 1986. Wang explained that this was due to the steady diminution of “ethnic contradictions” since 1949, so that by the mid-1980s they had vanished, thus no longer warranting special mention (Wang, 2000, pp. 393–4, cited in Jones, 2005, p. 85). Nevertheless, textual content belied this confidence, with the definition of Chinese “national heroes” (民族英雄) reconfigured to embrace Genghis Khan and exclude Yue Fei, and prominence accorded to “the peaceful liberation of Tibet” (Jones, 2005, p. 85). Wang herself clearly continued to believe that the vision of a “multi-ethnic” China required vigorous promotion, as the content of the 1992 texts testifies.

* The 1980s saw political and social changes in China, including a relaxation of constraints on cultural and religious expression and the implementation of policies and laws to protect minorities' cultural and religious rights
* The Nationalities and Regional Autonomy Law was enacted in 1984 to strengthen protection for minorities' "cultural autonomy"
* Fei Xiaotong proposed a conception of Chinese nationhood characterized by "diversity in unity" in 1988, which was later adopted as an official policy principle
* The 1988 draft Outline for History at the junior secondary level allocated 5% of class hours to the teaching of ethnic minority or local history
* The 1992 junior secondary history textbooks were based on this outline and were published by the People's Education Press (PEP)
* The 2002 edition of the textbooks was a revision of the 1992 edition and remained in use until 2016

Alternatively, Mr Campbell submitted that Mr Boulus and Mr McCarthy are not “persons” for the purposes of s 37 of the Act.

Neither Mr Boulus nor Mr McCarthy is currently a party to the proceedings. Mr Campbell did not appear for Mr McCarthy. Mr Campbell did not dispute that the Builder itself is a “person” for the purposes of s 37 of the Act.

In Pafburn, I held that a person “having substantive control over the carrying out of any work” for the purpose of cl (d) of the definition of “construction work” in s 36(1) of the Act included a person able to control how the work was carried out. [14]

14. At [26].

In the proposed Technology and Construction Cross-Claim List Statement, the Council alleges that Mr Boulus and Mr McCarthy were both able to, and in fact did, exercise control over the carrying out of the building work.

Thus, it is alleged that:

“ … [i]n his capacity as the managing director of [the Builder], [Mr Boulus] had the power and ability to and did substantively control all of the building works comprising the entire project, such control including the appointment and control of the project delivery staff working for [the Builder] (including the appointment and control of [Mr McCarthy]), the supervision of the adequacy of the works performed by such project delivery staff, the selection and appointment of subcontractors to perform elements of the Works for which [the Builder] was ultimately responsible, and the overall supervision and acceptance of the works performed by [the Builder’s] employees and subcontractors, for the ultimate benefit of [the Council]. Further, as the managing director of [the Builder], [Mr Boulus] had the ultimate ability to control how the Works performed by [the Builder] were carried out.”

In relation to Mr McCarthy, it is alleged:

“As the site supervisor for the Project, [Mr McCarthy] actively supervised, coordinated and project managed all of the primary elements of the building works comprising the project, and coordinated and directed how the Works performed by [the Builder] were carried out, including by directing and engaging with [the Builder’s] subcontractors in the performance of their works.”

Mr Campbell pointed to the potentially wide-ranging consequences of construing “persons” in s 37 to cover a director of a builder, such as Mr Boulus, or an employee of a builder, such as Mr McCarthy.

Thus, Mr Campbell submitted:

“Every person on a construction site has substantive control or supervision over some building work performed at that site, often the work that they themselves directly perform, and accordingly, taking section 37 at its broadest interpretation, every such person could potentially come within the ambit of a ‘person who carries out construction work’, and be the subject of an automatic statutory duty of care to the current and future owners of a project where no such duty previously existed. Such a broad interpretation could make hundreds, or on a very large job even thousands, of people personally liable in respect of the construction work over which they have control or supervision, which would have far reaching and negative impacts on the construction industry.

When one considers the fact that construction cases often involve claims for hundreds of defects, which may involve the work of multiple subcontractors, consultants, and supervisors in addition to employees and officers of the builder, a broad interpretation of section 37 would also result in building cases that balloon to include huge numbers of defendants, increasing the cost and complexity of what is already a costly and complex area of litigation. This is especially so when one considers the potential for the defence of proportionate liability that can be pleaded in defence of a claim under [the Act] to raise the same issues of liability of multiple third parties even if the plaintiff does not join all potential defendants to their claim.” (Emphasis in original.)

In those circumstances, Mr Campbell submitted that “persons” should be construed more narrowly.

Mr Campbell submitted that the reference in s 37 to a “person” who carries out “construction work”, when read with the definition of “construction work” in s 36, is:

“… obviously intended to refer to more than just a builder, and by reference to their function encompasses roles such as the architect, the project manager, the design consultants and possibly sub-contractors…”.

Mr Campbell submitted that “person” should be construed as “a person who carries out construction work in their own capacity”, and as not including a person who acts as agent for another.

In the Second Reading Speech [15] delivered by the Minister on introduction of the Design and Building Practitioners Bill 2019, the Minister said that the Bill was designed “to introduce a suite of new obligations on design and building practitioners to ensure that each step of construction is well documented and compliant”. The Minister continued that the Bill introduces “a number of new requirements, which will ensure that key practitioners are held accountable for their work across planning, design and construction stages.”

15. New South Wales Legislative Council, Parliamentary Debates (Hansard), 19 November 2019 at 1776 (Damien Tudehope, Minister for Finance and Small Business).

The Minister also said, speaking of the clause in the Bill that became s 37 of the Act:

“For the first time in New South Wales, [s 37] establishes a statutory duty of care that eradicates any uncertainty that may exist in the common law that a duty is owed to the end user and in respect to liability for defective building work. Any person who carries out construction work will, under the provisions of the bill and for the first time, have an automatic duty to exercise reasonable care to avoid economic loss caused by defects in or related to a building for which the construction work is done or arising out of that work.” (Emphasis added.)

As the Minister, here, did no more than recite the language of the relevant clause, this passage casts no light on the question before me.

The “uncertainty” to which the Minister referred arose from the decision of the High Court in Brookfield Multiplex Ltd v Owners Corporation Strata Plan 61288. [16] In that case, the Court found that, in the particular circumstances before it, the owners corporation could not maintain a claim in negligence against the builder as successor in title to the developer. where is FTP in the osi 7 layer model?

FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is typically considered to be an application layer protocol in the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) 7-layer model. The OSI model defines a framework for computer communication that consists of seven layers:

1. Physical layer
2. Data Link layer
3. Network layer
4. Transport layer
5. Session layer
6. Presentation layer
7. Application layer

FTP is used to transfer files between hosts over a network, and it operates at the highest layer of the OSI model, the application layer. Other protocols that operate at this layer include HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), and Telnet.
where is SFTP in the osi 7 layer model?

It is used for secure file transfer over a network and it typically runs over the SSH (Secure Shell) protocol. SSH provides a secure encrypted connection between two hosts, and SFTP uses this connection to transfer files securely.

Like FTP, SFTP also operates at the highest layer of the OSI model, the application layer. So, SFTP is also considered to be an application layer protocol in the OSI 7-layer model.

As a Unity technical artist, I'd recommend the following steps to create the desired overlay effect using the camera stacking feature in Unity:

1. Create a new Unity project or open an existing one.
2. Create a new Shader by right-clicking in the Assets window, selecting "Create" > "Shader" > "Universal Render Pipeline" > "Unlit Shader Graph." Name the shader "GradientOverlay."
3. Double-click the GradientOverlay shader file to open it in the Shader Graph editor.
4. In the Shader Graph editor, create the following nodes:
	* Vector1: name it "Angle" (default value: 45)
	* Color: name it "ColorA" (set to the first color)
	* Color: name it "ColorB" (set to the second color)
	* Screen Position node
	* Split node (connect the RGBA output of the Screen Position node to the input of the Split node)
	* Divide node (connect the R output of the Split node to the A input, and the G output to the B input)
	* Subtract node (connect the output of the Divide node to the input)
	* Add node (connect the output of the Subtract node to the input)
	* Saturate node (connect the output of the Add node to the input)
	* Lerp node (connect the output of the Saturate node to the T input, ColorA to A input, and ColorB to B input)
	* Vector2: name it "TransparencyRange" (default value: 0.5, 1)
	* Remap node (connect the output of the Saturate node to the Input input, and set the Input Range as 0 to 1, and connect TransparencyRange to the Output Range)
	* Saturate node (connect the output of the Remap node to the input)
	* Vector1: name it "MaxTransparency" (default value: 0.5)
	* Multiply node (connect the output of the Saturate node to the A input, and MaxTransparency to the B input)
	* One Minus node (connect the output of the Multiply node to the input)
	* Alpha node (connect the output of the One Minus node to the input)
	* Color node (connect the output of the Lerp node to the Color input, and the output of the Alpha node to the Alpha input)
5. Connect the output of the Color node to the Unlit Master node's Color input.
6. Save the shader and close the Shader Graph editor.
7. Create a new Material in the Assets window, and assign the GradientOverlay shader to it.
8. Create a new Camera by right-clicking in the Hierarchy window and selecting "Camera." Name it "OverlayCamera."
9. Set the OverlayCamera's "Clear Flags" to "Don't Clear" and "Culling Mask" to "Nothing."
10. In the Hierarchy window, create a new UI canvas by right-clicking and selecting "UI" > "Canvas." Set the Canvas's "Render Mode" to "Screen Space - Camera" and assign the OverlayCamera to the "Render Camera" field.
11. Add an Image component to the Canvas. Set the "Source Image" field to "None" and change the "Material" field to the gradient overlay material you created earlier.
12. In the OverlayCamera settings, set the "Stacked" property to "Base Camera," assuming you have a base camera in the scene. If you don't, create a new Camera and set its "Clear Flags" to "Solid Color" and "Culling Mask" to "Everything."

Write a python script that takes a list of strings of format: “public class X” and looks for this string in a list of directories, and replaces it with “internal class X

You can use the following Python script to achieve this task. This script searches through the specified directories, and if a file contains the specified string, it will replace the string with the new format and save the updated file.
```python
import os
import re

def find_and_replace(dirs, target, replacement):
    for directory in dirs:
        for root, _, files in os.walk(directory):
            for file in files:
                if file.endswith('.swift'):
                    filepath = os.path.join(root, file)
                    with open(filepath, 'r') as f:
                        file_content = f.read()
                    
                    updated_content = re.sub(target, replacement, file_content)
                    
                    if file_content != updated_content:
                        with open(filepath, 'w') as f:
                            f.write(updated_content)
                        print(f"Updated {filepath}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    directories = ['/path/to/first/directory', '/path/to/second/directory']
    target_string = r'public class (\w+)'
    replacement_string = r'internal class \1'

    find_and_replace(directories, target_string, replacement_string)
```
Replace the `/path/to/first/directory` and `/path/to/second/directory` with the actual directory paths that you want to search in. You can add or remove directories in the `directories` list as needed. This script will search for `.swift` files in the specified directories and replace the target string with the replacement string.

A. To increase write performance
B. To prevent permission errors in opening the destination file
C. To guarantee atomicity of the data written to the destination
D. To save disk space

C. To guarantee atomicity of the data written to the destination.

Writing to a temporary file and then renaming it to the destination file is a common technique used to guarantee atomicity of the file update. The process of writing to a temporary file and renaming it ensures that the update to the file is either fully completed or not done at all. This helps to prevent partial or corrupted writes that could occur if the update process were interrupted due to a system crash or other error. This technique is often used for critical files or files that require consistency guarantees, such as database files.

Therefore, option C is the correct answer.

what is a .zprofile

`.zprofile` is a file that contains shell configurations and settings specific to the zsh shell. This file is sourced (i.e., executed) by zsh when it starts up, and it can be used to set environment variables, configure the shell prompt, define aliases, and perform other customizations.

The `.zprofile` file is similar to the `.bash_profile` file for the Bash shell. However, while `.bash_profile` is only sourced for login shells, `.zprofile` is sourced for both login and interactive shells. This means that any configurations or settings defined in `.zprofile` will apply to all zsh shells, whether you start them as login shells (e.g., by logging in to your Mac over SSH) or as interactive shells (e.g., by opening a terminal window).

Some common uses for the `.zprofile` file include:

* Setting environment variables that should be available to all zsh shells.
* Configuring the shell prompt to display useful information, such as the current working directory or the current Git branch.
* Defining aliases for commonly used commands.
* Setting up the PATH environment variable to include custom directories or binaries.

To create or edit your `.zprofile` file, you can use any text editor (e.g., `nano`, `vim`, `emacs`, or even `TextEdit`). The file should be located in your home directory (`~/`), and it will be automatically sourced by zsh when you start a new shell.

how does .bashrc differ from .bash\_profile differ

`.bashrc` and `.bash_profile` are both files that contain shell configurations and settings specific to the Bash shell, but they serve slightly different purposes.

`.bashrc` is sourced (i.e., executed) by Bash each time a new interactive shell is started, including new terminal windows or tabs. It is typically used to set environment variables, configure the shell prompt, define aliases, and perform other customizations that apply to interactive shells. The `.bashrc` file is specific to each user account and is stored in the user's home directory (`~/`).

`.bash_profile`, on the other hand, is sourced by Bash when a user logs in to their account (either locally or remotely over SSH). It is typically used to set up the user's environment, such as setting the PATH environment variable, defining system-wide aliases, or running scripts that should only be executed once per login. The `.bash_profile` file is also specific to each user account and is stored in the user's home directory (`~/`).

In practice, the distinction between `.bashrc` and `.bash_profile` can be a bit fuzzy, and some users may choose to merge the contents of both files into a single file (usually `.bashrc`). However, if you need to set up environment variables or customizations that should only apply to login shells, it's generally recommended to use `.bash_profile`. If you need to set up environment variables or customizations that should apply to all interactive shells, including login shells, you can put them in `.bashrc`.
what does rc mean in .bashrc?

The "rc" in `.bashrc` stands for "run commands". This naming convention is derived from the original Unix shell, the Bourne shell (`sh`), which used a file called `.profile` to run commands when the shell was started. The "rc" suffix was added to other shell configuration files to indicate that they too were designed to "run commands" when the shell was started or when certain events occurred.

In the case of Bash, the `.bashrc` file is sourced (i.e., executed) each time a new interactive shell is started. It contains commands and settings that are specific to the Bash shell and that should be applied to all interactive shells. By convention, the "rc" suffix is used to indicate that this file contains runtime configuration information that should be executed each time the shell starts up.

Other examples of files that use the "rc" naming convention in Unix-like systems include `.vimrc` (for configuring the Vim text editor) and `.screenrc` (for configuring the GNU Screen terminal multiplexer).

A Bayesian network is a probabilistic graphical model that represents a set of variables and their conditional dependencies using a directed acyclic graph (DAG). While DAGs do not allow for cyclic dependencies, it is possible to represent cyclic relationships using Bayesian networks by introducing latent (hidden) variables. Latent variables can be used to model the underlying causes of observed variables, allowing the Bayesian network to capture complex dependencies and relationships that may not be directly observed.

In addition, Bayesian networks can be used to model sequences of variable length by using dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs). A DBN is a type of Bayesian network that models temporal dependencies by introducing a time dimension to the graph. Each time step in the DBN corresponds to a slice in the graph, allowing the model to capture changes in the distribution of variables over time. Using DBNs, it is possible to model sequences of variable length by simply adding or removing slices from the DBN as needed.

Overall, Bayesian networks and dynamic Bayesian networks provide a flexible framework for modeling complex dependencies and relationships in data, including cyclic relationships and sequences of variable length.

Why would anyone use a database for sessions? JWT seems so much better and faster.

Both database-stored sessions and JWTs have their own advantages and disadvantages, which is why some developers prefer one approach over the other. Here's a brief comparison of the two:

**Database-stored sessions:**

Advantages:

1. Revoking sessions: With a database, you can easily revoke sessions by deleting the corresponding session record. This provides better control over user sessions and can be useful in cases where a user needs to be logged out immediately (e.g., account compromise).
2. Server-side control: All session data is stored server-side, which can offer better security since sensitive information is not exposed to the client.
3. Scalability: Database-stored sessions can be more easily managed in a distributed environment, with session data centralized and accessible by multiple server instances.

Disadvantages:

1. Performance: Database access adds latency to each request, as the session data needs to be fetched from the database. This can be mitigated by using caching mechanisms or in-memory databases like Redis.
2. Complexity: Managing sessions in a database requires additional setup, including configuring the database, handling migrations, and managing database connections.

**JWTs:**

Advantages:

1. Performance: JWTs are stored client-side, so there's no need to access a database to validate the user on each request. This reduces server load and improves performance.
2. Stateless: JWTs are self-contained tokens with all the necessary information to validate the user, making the system stateless and easier to scale horizontally.
3. Easier setup: JWTs do not require database setup or management, simplifying the authentication process.

Disadvantages:

1. Revoking tokens: It's difficult to revoke JWTs before they expire, as they are stored client-side and can be used for authentication as long as they're valid. One workaround is to use short-lived tokens and maintain a server-side blacklist of tokens that need to be revoked.
2. Token size: JWTs can become large if they store a lot of user information, which can increase the size of HTTP requests and responses.
3. Security: Since JWTs are stored client-side, there's a risk of exposure if an attacker manages to intercept the token. You should always use HTTPS to mitigate this risk.

In summary, the choice between database-stored sessions and JWTs depends on the specific requirements of your application and your priorities regarding security, performance, and scalability. Some developers prefer the better control over sessions and security offered by database-stored sessions, while others prefer the performance and simplicity of JWTs.
I switched to JWT tokens and now my server takes 15s to respond?

A 15-second server response time after switching to JWT tokens is not expected behavior, as JWT tokens should generally lead to better performance compared to database-stored sessions. There might be other factors causing the delay in your application. Here are some suggestions to help you investigate and resolve the issue:

1. **Check your JWT token size:** Large JWT tokens can increase the size of HTTP requests and responses, causing delays. Ensure that you're only storing the necessary information in the token. Keep in mind that JWTs are sent with each request, so minimizing the token size is important.
2. **Profile your application:** Use profiling tools or built-in Next.js metrics to identify bottlenecks in your application. This will help you understand which parts of your application are causing the delay.
3. **Inspect your callbacks:** Double-check your `[...nextauth].js` configuration file, specifically the `jwt` and `session` callbacks. Make sure you're not performing any expensive operations or blocking calls within these callbacks.
4. **Review network requests:** Use the Network tab in your browser's developer tools to inspect the requests being made by your application. This will help you identify any requests that are taking an unusually long time to complete. If you find such requests, investigate the cause and optimize the corresponding API or resource.
5. **Check for external dependencies:** Ensure that any external dependencies, such as third-party APIs, are not causing the delay. Slow external requests can significantly impact the performance of your application.
6. **Optimize server-side code:** Review your server-side code for any performance issues, such as inefficient database queries, unoptimized algorithms, or unnecessary blocking operations. Optimize your code to improve the overall performance of your application.
7. **Verify server resources:** Make sure your server has sufficient resources (CPU, memory, and network bandwidth) to handle the traffic and workload. If your server is running low on resources, it might lead to slow response times.
8. **Check for rate limiting:** Some services, such as the Google OAuth API, have rate limits that might slow down your application if you exceed the allowed number of requests. Verify that you're not exceeding the rate limits imposed by any of the services you're using.

By investigating and addressing these potential issues, you should be able to improve the response time of your server after switching to JWT tokens.

create an Excel macro to go through all worksheets in a workbook do the following: bold the first row, center the text on the first row, and freeze the first row

Here is an example of a macro that will accomplish the task you described:
```vbnet
Sub FormatFirstRow()
  Dim ws As Worksheet
  For Each ws In ThisWorkbook.Worksheets
    With ws
      .Rows(1).Font.Bold = True
      .Rows(1).HorizontalAlignment = xlCenter
      .Rows(1).Select
      .Range("1:1").Select
      .Application.ActiveWindow.FreezePanes = True
    End With
  Next ws
End Sub
```
To use this macro, you'll need to open the "Visual Basic Editor" in Excel (press `Alt + F11`), create a new module (right-click on a project in the Project Explorer, then select "Insert" > "Module"), and paste the code into the module. Explain at the level of nix newcomer how recursive dependency hashing works

Recursive dependency hashing is a mechanism used by the Nix package manager to ensure that all dependencies of a package are correctly built and available before building the package itself.

To explain this concept, let's start with the basics of how Nix works. In Nix, each package is described by a file called a "Nix expression" (or just "expression" for short). Each expression specifies the dependencies of the package, as well as how to build the package.

When Nix builds a package, it first reads the expression for that package to determine its dependencies. It then recursively reads the expressions for each of those dependencies, and so on, until it has a complete list of all the packages needed to build the original package.

At this point, Nix creates a "dependency graph" that represents the relationships between all the packages. The nodes in the graph are the packages themselves, and the edges represent the dependencies between them.

Once the dependency graph is constructed, Nix uses a hashing algorithm to compute a unique identifier (or "hash") for each package in the graph, based on the contents of its expression file and the hashes of its dependencies. This ensures that if any of the dependencies change, the hash of the package that depends on them will also change.

This is where the recursive aspect of dependency hashing comes in. When Nix calculates the hash for a package, it first calculates the hashes of all its dependencies. But if any of those dependencies have dependencies of their own, Nix recursively calculates the hashes of those dependencies as well. This continues until Nix has calculated the hashes of all the packages needed to build the original package.

In summary, recursive dependency hashing is a mechanism used by Nix to ensure that all dependencies of a package are correctly built and available before building the package itself. It works by recursively calculating the hashes of all the packages in the dependency graph, based on the contents of their expression files and the hashes of their dependencies.

The main difference between the Dockerfile approach and the Nix approach to making container images is that Dockerfiles specify the exact steps to build an image, while the Nix approach uses a declarative language to define the dependencies and configuration of the image.

In the Dockerfile approach, the developer writes a series of instructions that are executed in order to build an image. This can include installing dependencies, copying files, and setting environment variables. The resulting image is built based on these instructions and can be deployed to any system that can run Docker.

On the other hand, the Nix approach uses a declarative language to describe the dependencies and configuration of the image. This includes specifying which packages should be installed and how they should be configured. The resulting image is built by running a Nix expression that defines the dependencies and configuration of the image.

One advantage of the Nix approach is that it allows for reproducible builds, where the same image can be built on different systems and the resulting image will be identical. This is because the Nix expression specifies the exact dependencies and configuration of the image, rather than relying on a set of instructions that may have different results on different systems.

Another advantage of the Nix approach is that it integrates well with the Nix package manager, which provides a large collection of pre-built packages that can be easily included in the image. This can save time and effort compared to manually installing dependencies in a Dockerfile.

Overall, the Nix approach to building container images provides a more declarative and reproducible way to define dependencies and configuration, while the Dockerfile approach is more flexible and allows for more customization.

According to Rand, self-interest is the only rational way for a person to act and is not only moral, but necessary in order for an individual to thrive. She argued that selflessness—which altruism promotes—is self-defeating and leads to an individual's self-destruction. In other words, Rand believes that humans should pursue their own self-interests in order to achieve a successful life. 
Rand's perspective conflicts with traditional views of altruism, which promote selflessness and consider it the ultimate moral act. According to Rand, selfless behavior is a form of self-sacrifice and ultimately leads to an individual's self-destruction. On the other hand, self-interest is seen by Rand as being necessary for survival and success.

class StackedLSTM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, output_size):
        super(StackedLSTM, self).__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.num_layers = num_layers

        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(hidden_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size)

    def forward(self, x, lengths):
        x = self.embedding(x)
        x = pack_padded_sequence(x, lengths, batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False)
        out, _ = self.lstm(x)
        out, _ = pad_packed_sequence(out, batch_first=True)
        out = self.fc(out)
        return out

When building a new home, homeowners may encounter latent conditions that were not accounted for in the original scope of work or building contract. Some common examples of latent conditions in new builds include:

* Presence of asbestos or other hazardous materials in the soil or existing structures on the site
* Poor site drainage or unstable land that can affect the stability of the foundation or building structure
* Unexpected changes to local building codes or regulations that require additional work or modifications to the design

These latent conditions can significantly impact the construction process and budget, potentially leading to delays and cost overruns. In some cases, latent conditions may require significant changes to the original design or scope of work, leading to disputes between homeowners and builders.

To protect their legal rights, homeowners should be aware of their contractual obligations and the legal remedies available to them. A well-drafted building contract should include provisions for dealing with latent conditions, including how additional costs will be allocated and any necessary changes to the scope of work or design.

In general, homeowners have a legal right to be informed of any latent conditions that may impact the construction process or budget. Builders have a duty to disclose any known latent conditions, and homeowners should be proactive in identifying potential issues and discussing them with their builder early in the construction process.

When latent conditions are encountered, homeowners should seek the advice of a professional, such as a construction lawyer or building expert, to understand their legal rights and options for resolving disputes with their builder. In some cases, it may be possible to negotiate a variation to the contract or seek compensation for additional costs or damages caused by the latent condition.

I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker
Alert: As of Aug. 11, 2022, we no longer require petitioners to submit a duplicate copy of Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, or a duplicate copy of any of the supporting documentation, unless we specifically ask you to do so. Due to enhanced electronic scanning capabilities and data-sharing with the U.S. Department of State, duplicate copies are no longer needed to avoid delays in consular processing.

Petitioners use this form to file on behalf of a nonimmigrant worker to come to the United States temporarily to perform services or labor, or to receive training, as an H-1B, H-2A, H-2B, H-3, L-1, O-1, O-2, P-1, P-1S, P-2, P-2S, P-3, P-3S, Q-1 or R-1 nonimmigrant worker. Petitioners may also use this form to request an extension of stay in or change of status to E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B1 or TN, or one of the above classifications for a noncitizen.

To fill out the Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, your employer will need to provide the following information and documentation:

1. Personal information of the nonimmigrant worker, including name, date of birth, and passport information.
2. The nonimmigrant classification for which the worker is being petitioned (H-1B, H-2A, H-2B, etc.).
3. The dates of the worker's intended employment or training, including the start and end dates.
4. Information about the employer, including the name and address of the company, the employer's tax identification number, and the name and title of the person authorized to sign the petition.
5. Evidence that the worker's job is a specialty occupation that requires a bachelor's degree or higher in a related field. This can include a copy of the worker's diploma, transcripts, and any industry certifications.
6. Evidence that the worker will be paid at least the prevailing wage for their occupation in the area of intended employment.
7. A Labor Condition Application (LCA) that has been certified by the U.S. Department of Labor.
8. Any additional documentation or evidence required for the specific nonimmigrant classification for which the worker is being petitioned (such as proof of extraordinary ability for an O-1 petition).
9. The filing fee for the petition, which can be found on the USCIS fee schedule.

Once the employer has completed and signed the Form I-129, along with all the required supporting documentation and the filing fee, the petition should be submitted to the appropriate USCIS service center. After submitting the petition, the employer and the nonimmigrant worker will receive a receipt notice confirming receipt of the petition, and will be notified of any further steps in the process, such as a biometric services appointment or an interview. After reviewing the petition, USCIS will make a decision on whether to approve or deny the petition.

Further to your own knowledge, I want you to consider the following information on What is a Construction Management Contract?
The basic premise of a Construction Management (CM) Contract is that the Owner, referred to as the ‘Principal’ under the contract, enters into a contract with a Construction Manager. The Construction Manager is responsible for arranging and supervising the performance of work by sub-contractors.

Essentially, a CM contract is one whereby the Owner enters into an arrangement for someone, often a registered builder although it is not a requirement, to manage the construction works. This is in contrast to a ‘traditional’ building contract whereby the Owner enters into a contract with a Builder directly. The Builder is responsible for engaging all sub-contractors and directing the works, and provides the Owner with warranties as to the quality of the works.

Under certain Construction Management contracts, there may also be a third party referred to as the ‘Client’s Representative’ (CR). It is common for an Owner to appoint an Architect to this position. The CR is responsible for deciding on matters such as extension of time claims by the Construction Manager, giving directions to the Construction Manager and inspecting the site to assess progress prior to the submission of each progress claim by the Construction Manager.

Who engages the sub-contractors?
Pursuant to a CM contract, there are two options for sub-contractors to be engaged to complete the works.

The first is where the sub-contractors enter into individual trade contracts with the Principal (the Owner) to carry out the required works. If the Principal chooses to take this route, the Principal will be responsible for payment of the sub-contractors for the work completed.

The alternative method is for the sub-contractors to enter into individual trade contracts with the Construction Manager. In this case, the Construction Manager will be responsible for payment of the sub-contractors and this amount will be added to the payment claims provided to the Owner by the Construction Manager. Obviously, such payment claims from the Construction Manager must include supporting verification of claims by the trades.

What happens if there are defective works?
Each of the trade contracts entered into with the sub-contractors will contain provisions relating to defect liability periods and warranties for work performed. Therefore, it is important to carefully consider the provisions of each individual trade contract and to obtain expert legal advice before entering into such contracts.

Depending upon the terms of the CM contract, it is possible that the Construction Manager will also provide warranties for defective work by a sub-contractor. It is, however, far more likely that the CM contract will contain a provision expressly stating that the Construction Manager will not be liable to the Owner for any acts or omissions by the sub-contractors. If that is the case, then the Owner will only have a claim against the individual sub-contractors for any defective work.

Notwithstanding the inclusion of any provision similar to that described above, the Construction Manager can be liable to the Owner for any breach of the CM contract or for failing to properly manage and arrange the carrying out of the works by the sub-contractors. There will be duties to the Owner spelt out in the CM contract and also a duty of care at common law.

Should I use a Construction Management contract?
While there are benefits to using a CM contract in certain situations, there are also risks involved as the Principal (the Owner) takes on many more risks than in a traditional building contract with a builder. This is particularly noteworthy if it is domestic rather than commercial construction.

If you are considering entering into a CM contract for your project, it is essential that you seek expert legal advice regarding the risks involved and the terms of the specific contract you are considering entering into.

Chapter 1. Geometry,
philosophy and world order:
the episode before 1200
There was no mathematical practice in the ancient cultures, and neither was it to materialise until
about 1200. This might be a devastating start of a book about 2500 years of mathematical
practices: most of the time within these two-and-a-half millennia, there was no mathematical
practice. Yet there must have been something, for mathematical practices didn’t emerge from
scratch. And indeed, within the various cultures in Europe, there was knowledge that we today
might recognise as mathematical, and these contained the seeds of what later would become
mathematics.
In all the ancient views there was one constant that drove these mathematical sparks, and that
was esoteric knowledge. Mysticism, trying to understand the intention of the Gods or God, finding
out what the future held, these were all motivations for attempting to describe in number
or lines, the works that we would today consider as mathematics. For example, to the Babylonian
and Egypt priests and scribes, knowledge of number, including numerology, and astrology were
part of the requirements needed to function within the temple administration. Just like writing
and performing certain rituals, one had to be able to do some basic surveying and accounting
work. There was no-one who called himself or was called a mathematician and it is even
doubtful whether the various techniques that we today would consider mathematical were even
viewed as belonging together in any particular way. The Pythagorean theorem was used by both
Babylonian priests as Egyptian scribes, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that it was anything
else but a rule of thumb, to help out in certain situations. The fact that numbers were so often
connected to specific situations in rituals, may even indicate that the certainty in using these ru-
Mathematical worlds 21
les were just as much revealed by the Gods, and thereby offered a similar kind of certainty as the
words of prophets or the laws issued by a king. In the Gilgamesh epos, for example, the numbers
seven and three are used frequently, to illustrate the divinity of the king. In the Old Testament
these same numbers play an important role, and it may even be read that “God ordered the
world to measure and number” (Salomon 11:20). The circle and the sphere were considered sacred
objects and thereby worthy of the attention of mortals. Drawing a horoscope from the stars
was as obvious as using these stars to calculate one’s position, or using them to calculate the
best time to sow or harvest crops. This doesn’t necessarily mean that no-one in ancient culture
recognised the differences between these rules, but in general people regarded knowledge as
wisdom, as something that had been revealed, and what inspired the particular interest in the
subjects that we would nowadays consider to be mathematics, was esoteric.
During the ancient Greek civilisation, however, a practice rose that did view these subjects as
something special. This practice was a group of philosophers, or that was what they were called,
sometimes also part of a sect or cult, and as the name suggests, their interest was much broader
than mathematics alone. They had words for geometria and arithmetica, which indicates that
they were aware of the fact that it was something that deserved a separate phrase. Both were
practical activities part of very local philosophical practices. Geometria was literally measuring
the world (γεω or geo means “earth”; the Greek μετρίᾳ or metria, “measure” but has “being modest”
as a second meaning) and that was the first step to measuring the stars: astrology or astronomy.
Arithmetica was a more mundane subject, associated also with merchants and administrating,
but the philosophers thought there was wisdom to be found in numbers as there was in
the stars. This wisdom was mundane but also of an esoteric nature.
Geometria and arithmetica were not regarded as true philosophy, but they did make up the simplest
examples of philosophising and were thereby at the very least of pedagogical importance
to the philosophers. The subjects were considered important by a small group of culturally and
politically privileged people, who could afford themselves time for contemplation. Within the
western world this small group of people was nevertheless decisive in many ways: politically,
economically and culturally. If only for that reason, in the following sections the Greek, Roman
and medieval Christian views on the subjects of geometria and arithmetica will be discussed.
Mathematics and myths: knowledge of the world
Thales of Myletus (ca. 624 – ca. 548) is often called the first mathematician. That is quite a title for
someone we know so little about. We know that he was a very rich merchant, therefor it is highly
probable that, once he had accumulated his wealth, he became politically active and could afford
himself some education. Philosophy, geometria and arithmetica as introduction to that, was
the obvious start. Trying to understand the world in a physical, political or mystical sense, and
selling that rhetorically, was the goal. According to a couple of Greek authors some century after
Mathematical worlds 22
him, he was the first to have formulated a proof for Thales’ theorem, but it is unknown what the
proof looked like. His fellow countrymen a century and a half later, however, were definitely
thinking highly of him, and of his attempt to proof the theorem. To Thales and his contemporaries,
geometria (to which the famous theorem belonged) was part of philosophy and part of the
studies that were to allow him the general knowledge that offered more insight into the way the
world was ordered. Knowledge of the divine reasons or interventions that determined both the
movement of the heavens (surveying, astronomy, astrology) and the way our direct surroundings
worked (geography, politics). It is with some hesitation that I do start a cultural history of
mathematics with Thales, for it might be that later authors projected more of their views of geometria,
on this ancient character.

The ancient cultures did not have mathematical practices as we know it today. Instead, mathematical knowledge was considered part of esoteric knowledge, used for purposes such as astrology and temple administration. During the ancient Greek civilization, a group of philosophers known as the Greek philosophers started to view mathematical subjects as separate from other subjects, and saw wisdom in both geometria and arithmetica. Thales of Myletus is often called the first mathematician, a wealthy merchant who became politically active and pursued education in philosophy, geometria, and arithmetica. Design an $O(n \log n)$ time algorithm to invert the Polar Transform, i.e., to compute $(x\_0,\ldots,x\_{n-1})$ given 
 $(w\_0,\ldots,w\_{n-1}) = P\_n(x\_0,\ldots,x\_{n-1})$. \\

To design an O(n log n) time algorithm to invert the Polar Transform, we can follow a similar divide-and-conquer strategy, similar to the algorithm used to compute the Polar Transform. Here’s a high-level outline of the algorithm:
1. Create a recursive function called `invert_polar_transform` that takes the transformed list `w` and the current level `l` as inputs. The base case is when `l = 0`, in which case the function should return the input list `w`.
2. If the current level `l` is not 0, divide the transformed list `w` into two equal halves: `w_left` and `w_right`.
3. Recursively apply the `invert_polar_transform` function to both halves, decrementing the level by 1: `x_left = invert_polar_transform(w_left, l - 1)` and `x_right = invert_polar_transform(w_right, l - 1)`.
4. Merge the results from `x_left` and `x_right` to obtain the original input list `x`. For each index `i` in the range `[0, 2^{l-1})`, compute the XOR of the corresponding elements in `x_left` and `x_right` and update `x_right` as follows: `x_right[i] = x_left[i] ⊕ x_right[i]`.
5. Concatenate `x_left` and `x_right` to obtain the final input list `x`. Return `x`.
This algorithm has a complexity of O(n log n), as it follows a divide-and-conquer strategy, dividing the problem into two equal halves at each level and merging the results.
Here is a Python implementation of the algorithm:

```java
def invert_polar_transform(w, l):
    if l == 0:
        return w
    
    n = len(w)
    w_left = w[:n//2]
    w_right = w[n//2:]
    
    x_left = invert_polar_transform(w_left, l - 1)
    x_right = invert_polar_transform(w_right, l - 1)
    
    for i in range(2**(l-1)):
        x_right[i] = x_left[i] ^ x_right[i]
    
    return x_left + x_right
```

We can design an algorithm for integer multiplication of two n-digit numbers where each number is split into three parts, each with n/3 digits, using a method similar to the Karatsuba algorithm. We’ll call this the “trinary multiplication algorithm”. Here is a high-level outline of the algorithm:
1. Given two n-digit numbers X and Y, split each number into three parts, each with n/3 digits:
	* X = A \* 10^(2 \* (n/3)) + B \* 10^(n/3) + C
	* Y = D \* 10^(2 \* (n/3)) + E \* 10^(n/3) + F
2. Calculate six multiplications between the smaller parts:
	* P1 = A \* D
	* P2 = B \* E
	* P3 = C \* F
	* P4 = (A + B) \* (D + E) - P1 - P2
	* P5 = (B + C) \* (E + F) - P2 - P3
	* P6 = (A + C) \* (D + F) - P1 - P3
3. Combine the multiplications P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, and P6 to calculate the product of X and Y:
	* Product = P1 \* 10^(4 \* (n/3)) + P4 \* 10^(3 \* (n/3)) + P6 \* 10^(2 \* (n/3)) + P5 \* 10^(n/3) + P3
Here’s the Python implementation of the trinary multiplication algorithm:

```java
def trinary_multiply(X, Y, n):
    if n == 1:
        return X * Y

    n_third = n // 3

    A = X // (10 ** (2 * n_third))
    B = (X // (10 ** n_third)) % (10 ** n_third)
    C = X % (10 ** n_third)

    D = Y // (10 ** (2 * n_third))
    E = (Y // (10 ** n_third)) % (10 ** n_third)
    F = Y % (10 ** n_third)

    P1 = trinary_multiply(A, D, n_third)
    P2 = trinary_multiply(B, E, n_third)
    P3 = trinary_multiply(C, F, n_third)
    P4 = trinary_multiply(A + B, D + E, n_third) - P1 - P2
    P5 = trinary_multiply(B + C, E + F, n_third) - P2 - P3
    P6 = trinary_multiply(A + C, D + F, n_third) - P1 - P3

    return (P1 * (10 ** (4 * n_third)) +
            P4 * (10 ** (3 * n_third)) +
            P6 * (10 ** (2 * n_third)) +
            P5 * (10 ** n_third) +
            P3)
```

The following SQL statement can be used to show Employee names with their associated address information, assuming that the foreign key from the Employee table to the Address table is named "address\_id":
```
SELECT Employee.name, Address.* 
FROM Employee
INNER JOIN Address ON Employee.address_id = Address.id;
```
This statement uses an INNER JOIN to combine the rows from the Employee and Address tables where the value of the address\_id column in the Employee table matches the value of the id column in the Address table. Electronic countermeasures (ECM) are techniques used to prevent or disrupt communication systems, particularly in the context of military or defense applications. In mobile communications, ECM is often used to prevent or mitigate the effects of intentional interference, such as jamming.

Conventional electronic countermeasures in mobile communications include:

1. Frequency hopping: This technique involves rapidly switching between different frequency channels in a pre-determined sequence. This can make it difficult for a jammer to disrupt the communication, as the signal is constantly changing frequency.
2. Spread spectrum: This technique spreads the signal across a wide frequency range. By doing so, it reduces the power density of the signal, making it less susceptible to jamming.
3. Directional antennas: By using directional antennas, the signal can be focused in a specific direction, making it harder for a jammer to disrupt the communication.
4. Power control: This technique involves dynamically adjusting the power of the transmitter to maintain a consistent signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). By doing so, it makes it more difficult for a jammer to overpower the signal with noise.
5. Error correction codes: These codes can be used to detect and correct errors in the received signal. By doing so, the system can recover from interference and maintain communication.

These techniques are often used in combination to provide robust anti-jamming capabilities in mobile communication systems.

* Random Noise Jamming: This type of jamming involves adding random noise to the intended signal to disrupt communication.
* Pulse Jamming: This type of jamming involves transmitting pulses of high power noise to disrupt communication.

To counteract these jamming techniques, ECM techniques such as frequency hopping, spread spectrum, directional antennas, power control, and error correction codes can be employed. Frequency hopping and spread spectrum are two related techniques used in wireless communication, but they are not the same thing.

Frequency hopping is a technique where a radio rapidly switches its transmitting frequency over a pre-defined sequence of frequencies, with each frequency used for only a short period of time. This sequence is known only to the communicating parties and can be changed frequently to make it difficult for an adversary to jam the signal. Frequency hopping is a form of spread spectrum, as it spreads the signal over a range of frequencies.

Spread spectrum is a technique where a signal is spread over a range of frequencies, rather than being transmitted on a single frequency. This is done by modulating the signal using a spreading code that is independent of the data being transmitted.
